title: Bayes' Theorem: How to Change Your Mind Without Losing It
subtitle: New evidence lands. How much should it move you? There's an exact answer — and it's the most useful formula you'll ever internalize.
hook: You test positive for a scary-but-rare disease on a test that's '99% accurate.' Panic? Actually… probably not. The math says you're likely fine — and the reason is the single most powerful thinking tool in this whole track: **Bayes' theorem**. It's the rule for updating a belief when new evidence arrives. Yesterday's boss question hinted at it; today we make it click. Master this and you'll stop being fooled by scary headlines and shiny data.

sections.heading: Start with the base rate
sections.body:
Bayes' big idea: **your new belief depends on what you believed before.** Before any test, how common is the disease? Say **1 in 1,000**. That starting number is the **base rate** (or 'prior'), and ignoring it is the classic blunder.

Evidence doesn't overwrite your prior — it *nudges* it. A positive test makes the disease more likely than 1-in-1,000, but if the disease was fantastically rare to begin with, 'more likely' can still be 'probably not.'

sections.heading: Why an accurate test still lies
sections.body:
Picture 1,000 people. **1** actually has the disease. The test is 99% accurate, so among the 999 healthy people it wrongly flags about **10** (1% false positives). So now ~11 people test positive — but only **1** is truly sick.

Your odds of being sick given a positive test? Roughly **1 in 11 ≈ 9%.** Not 99%. The rareness of the disease drowns the test's accuracy in false alarms. That's Bayes in one gut-punch.

sections.label: The one-line version
sections.body: **New belief ∝ (how likely the evidence is if true) × (how likely it was true to begin with).** Rare things need *strong* evidence to become likely. It's not that the test is bad — it's that you must weigh it against how rare the thing was. Doctors, juries, and investors get this wrong constantly.

takeaways: Bayes updates a belief with evidence — it **nudges your prior**, doesn't replace it.
The **base rate** (how common it is to begin with) is the piece people forget.
For rare things, even an accurate test yields mostly **false positives**.
Belief ∝ likelihood of the evidence × prior probability.
Rare claims demand **strong** evidence before you should believe them.

options: How common the thing is before any evidence
quiz.explain: It's your starting probability (prior). Ignoring it is the base-rate fallacy.

quiz.q: A 99%-accurate test, disease is 1-in-1,000, you test positive. Roughly your chance of being sick?
quiz.explain: ~1 real case vs ~10 false alarms among positives → about 1-in-11 ≈ 9%. Rareness dominates.

options: Always weigh new evidence against the base rate — that's what Bayes formalizes

tg_quiz.q: Rare disease (1/1000), 99%-accurate test, you test positive. Chance you're actually sick?
tg_quiz.correct: Exactly — ~9%. False positives swamp the rare true case.
